title: Justice Department Sues California to Block Counting 20,000 Alleged Noncitizen Ballots
excerpt: Filed hours after a 48-hour deadline expired, the suit asks a Los Angeles judge to set aside mail ballots from voters the administration calls likely noncitizens until citizenship is verified; California officials say the list is unverifiable and the demand unlawful.
body:
• The Justice Department sued California on October 15, asking a federal judge in Los Angeles to stop the state counting mail ballots from more than 20,000 voters the administration says are likely noncitizens, until their citizenship is verified.
  • The suit came hours after a 48-hour deadline expired; the list was delivered to Los Angeles County on a thumb drive that county officials said they had not opened, citing data privacy and security protocols.
  • California's Secretary of State Shirley Weber said the list was never sent to her office and lacks the detail to be of investigative use; Governor Gavin Newsom called the suit an attempt to suppress California voters three weeks before the November 3 midterms.
  • For naturalized citizens in California: your ballot is not cancelled by this lawsuit. If your ballot is set aside for verification, respond promptly to any notice from your county elections office so your citizenship can be confirmed and your vote counted.

The U.S. Justice Department sued California on Thursday, October 15, asking a federal judge to block the state from counting mail ballots for the November 3 midterm elections from more than 20,000 voters the Trump administration alleges are likely noncitizens, Reuters reported. The complaint, filed in the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California, asks the court to order the ballots set aside until each voter's citizenship status is determined.

A thumb drive, a 48-hour deadline, then court

On October 13, the department gave California 48 hours to review a list of alleged noncitizen voters and act, according to Al Jazeera. The list reached the Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder's office on a thumb drive with a handwritten note giving a password. County officials said they had not accessed the device, citing data privacy and security protocols. Secretary of State Shirley Weber said no list was ever sent to her office. When the deadline passed, the department filed suit. The Justice Department's statement, issued the same day, said it worked with the Department of Homeland Security, which compared publicly available California voter-registration files with federal immigration data; read the Justice Department statement on the California voter list suit for its account of the analysis.

https://x.com/JohnBasham/status/2110836164655468662

"State-facilitated voter fraud is unacceptable in the United States of America."

— Attorney General Todd Blanche, announcing the lawsuit

California's response

Weber said the department was demanding unprecedented measures based on unverifiable information, that the list lacked the detail to be of investigative use. Her office said California law already requires that only U.S. citizens register and that ineligible registrants are removed. Governor Gavin Newsom called the suit a desperate attempt to suppress California voters just three weeks before Election Day and said the state would defend free and fair elections. California began mailing ballots to all registered voters on October 5, so many of the ballots at issue are already in voters' hands.

The legal obstacles the suit faces

Elections in the United States are administered by the states, and legal experts quoted by Reuters, USA Today and CNN were skeptical. UCLA law professor Rick Hasen said the request could put California in conflict with a federal law barring mass voter-roll purges within 90 days of an election, and questioned federal authority to tell a state which ballots it may count. Notre Dame professor Derek Muller called the case a long shot, noting there is no federal law dictating how states verify citizenship on their rolls. Reuters also reported the department has sued 30 states and Washington, D.C. over voter-roll access and lost 26 of those cases without winning one. A Reuters investigation in July found 129 prosecutions for noncitizen voting since 1996, and advocates warn outdated federal data can wrongly flag naturalized citizens. Full background is in USA Today's coverage of the DOJ suit.

What this means for Indian-American and naturalized voters

California has one of the largest Indian-American populations in the United States, and most Indian-American voters are naturalized citizens — the group advocates say is most at risk of being wrongly matched against older records. Being named on a federal list is an allegation, not a finding: the suit asks for ballots to be held pending verification, not cancelled. Check your registration through the Secretary of State's voter portal, return your ballot as usual, and answer any county verification notice quickly so a held ballot can be released and counted.

What happens next

A judge in Los Angeles must now decide whether to grant emergency relief with voting already under way and the election on November 3. California officials have said they will defend the state's election process in court. A parallel lawsuit filed the same day by voting-rights groups challenges the federal collection of state voter records, making this one front in a wider fight over federal access to voter data.
